meta.title: VPN blog: setup, protocols, speed
meta.description: Guides to setting up a VPN on iPhone, Android, Windows, macOS and a router, what to do when a VPN will not connect, and how Hysteria2 and VLESS Reality work.

title: Blog
intro: Step-by-step guides for phones, computers, televisions and routers, a look at the protocols, and why a VPN sometimes refuses to connect. No marketing — only what we have tested on our own infrastructure.
cta: GnomeVPN runs Hysteria2 and VLESS + Reality side by side: if one does not work on a network, the connection goes over the other. One subscription for every device.

hysteria2-vs-vless.title: Hysteria2 or VLESS + Reality: what differs and which to pick
hysteria2-vs-vless.excerpt: Two protocols solve one problem in opposite ways. One holds its speed under packet loss, the other works where UDP is closed.
hysteria2-vs-vless.intro: Both protocols give you a private connection, and they are built on opposite principles. Hysteria2 runs over UDP and wins on unstable networks. VLESS + Reality runs over TCP with the TLS handshake of a real site and works where UDP is dropped outright. Here is when to use which.

whatIsHysteria.title: What Hysteria2 is
whatIsHysteria.body: Hysteria2 is a protocol built on QUIC, the transport Google designed for HTTP/3. QUIC runs over UDP and does something TCP cannot: it recovers a lost packet without stalling the whole stream. In TCP a single lost packet holds up everything queued behind it — head-of-line blocking. On a wired connection the difference is invisible, but on a mobile network, where 2-5% loss is ordinary, it decides everything. On top of that, TLS 1.3 encryption is built into QUIC itself, so a connection is set up faster than with a VPN over TCP.

whatIsReality.title: What VLESS + Reality is
whatIsReality.body: Reality is not a protocol of its own but a way of setting up the TLS connection for VLESS. An ordinary TLS-based VPN needs a domain and a certificate of its own — self-signed or issued for that domain. Reality works differently: the server carries out the TLS handshake with the certificate of a real third-party site, and a key only your app knows tells your connection apart from the rest. That is why VLESS + Reality works where only HTTPS on port 443 is open.

packetLoss.title: Packet loss: where Hysteria2 wins
packetLoss.body: Mobile networks lose packets constantly — handing over between towers, weak signal, a congested cell. Over TCP that shows up as speed collapsing in waves, because the connection keeps waiting on retransmission. QUIC in Hysteria2 handles each stream independently, so a loss in one does not hold up the rest. In practice the difference shows wherever loss exceeds 1-2%: on the underground, on a train, on crowded Wi-Fi. That is why Hysteria2 is first in our server list.

blocking.title: Strict networks: where Reality wins
blocking.body: Hysteria2 has one weak point — it runs over UDP, and UDP is often dropped wholesale. Corporate networks, hotel Wi-Fi and a few carriers pass only TCP on ports 80 and 443. There Hysteria2 cannot come up at all, however it is configured. Reality rides TCP on port 443 — the port every HTTPS site uses — so it works on those networks. The other side of that: TCP copes worse with packet loss, and on an unstable network VLESS loses more speed.

howToChoose.title: What to pick in practice
howToChoose.body: Start with Hysteria2 — the app labels each entry with its protocol. On most networks it is faster and steadier. If the connection will not establish, or drops immediately, switch to the VLESS entry for the same country, which is Reality. Nothing needs configuring: both servers are already in the subscription and the app remembers your choice. If neither works, the problem is usually the network rather than the protocol — try mobile data instead of Wi-Fi.

vpn-not-working-hotel-wifi.title: The VPN will not work in a hotel or at the office: what to do
vpn-not-working-hotel-wifi.excerpt: Public and corporate networks filter more than you would expect. Here is each cause and what to do about it.
vpn-not-working-hotel-wifi.intro: Everything works at home, and then in a hotel or an office the VPN will not connect. The cause is almost always that the network filters traffic — but it filters in different ways, and the fix depends on which.

whyItFails.title: Why these networks specifically
whyItFails.body: A home provider usually does not restrict protocols or ports. A corporate network works the other way round: what the administrator explicitly opened is allowed and nothing else. Hotel Wi-Fi sits closer to the corporate model — the owner wants no trouble and closes everything surplus. In both cases the filter is not aimed at VPNs in particular; the rule is simply "leave the web working". The side effect is that a VPN stops working alongside games, video calls and anything else that does not look like a browser.

udpBlocked.title: The usual cause: UDP is blocked
udpBlocked.body: Protocols like Hysteria2 and WireGuard run over UDP. To a network administrator UDP is something that has to be allowed deliberately: browsing works without it, and it brings volume and trouble. So the filter often keeps only TCP on ports 80 and 443. The tell for this cause: the connection never establishes at all, the app keeps trying and gives up on a timeout. There is no authentication error, because the packets never reach the server.

switchToTcp.title: The fix: switch to TCP
switchToTcp.body: In a GnomeVPN subscription every country comes in several variants. The main one is Hysteria2 over UDP, the fallback is VLESS + Reality over TCP; the app labels each entry with its protocol. The second rides TCP on port 443 — the same channel as any HTTPS site. A network that lets a browser through lets it through too. Switching takes one tap in the app and nothing has to be reconfigured. If the TCP entry connects, UDP was the cause, and that is the entry to use on this network.

captivePortal.title: The second cause: a captive portal
captivePortal.body: Many public networks demand sign-in first: open a browser, accept the terms, sometimes enter a room number. Until that is done the network intercepts everything and lets nothing out. A VPN will not connect at that point even where the protocol is allowed. It is easy to check — open any site over plain HTTP. If you land on the hotel page, sign in there first and turn the VPN on afterwards. The order matters: some apps need restarting once the portal has let you through.

stillStuck.title: If none of that helped
stillStuck.body: Two possibilities remain. The first is to tether from a phone: mobile networks almost never filter UDP, and ordinary Hysteria2 works there. The second is that the network runs deep packet inspection and blocks on content rather than on ports. That is rare and mostly confined to large companies with a serious security team. There is little to be done about it from the client side, and it is more honest to accept that a VPN will not work on that network.

vpn-android-tv.title: Setting up a VPN on Android TV and Apple TV
vpn-android-tv.excerpt: A TV has no browser and no usable keyboard. Here is how to add the subscription by QR code in about a minute.
vpn-android-tv.intro: A television is the most awkward device to configure — typing a long link with a remote is painful. The good news is that you do not have to: it all goes through a QR code shown on a phone.

whatYouNeed.title: What you need
whatYouNeed.body: A television running Android TV (Sony, Philips, Xiaomi, most recent sets) or an Apple TV. A phone with your account open — it is only there to display the QR code. And an active subscription: without one the servers appear in the list but the connection fails authentication. Sets running Tizen (Samsung) or webOS (LG) will not work — there is no app for them, and neither system offers a supported way to install a VPN.

installing.title: Installing the app
installing.body: On Android TV open Google Play on the television itself and search for INCY. Where Play is unavailable the app can be sideloaded from an APK, but that needs a file manager and installation from unknown sources enabled, which is considerably more work. On Apple TV the app is in the App Store, found the same way as on an iPhone. Installation takes under a minute and the app needs no account of its own — it is free and works with any subscription.

addingSubscription.title: Adding the subscription by QR
addingSubscription.body: In the app on the television choose to add a subscription and pick the QR option — either the camera starts or a field for the code appears. Now open your account on your phone: the Connect tab, «With a link», your app — and press QR code. Hold the phone screen up to the television: the app reads the link and pulls in every server by itself.

remoteControl.title: When there is no camera
remoteControl.body: Some televisions have no camera and cannot scan a QR code at all. Then the link has to be typed with the remote — tedious, but only once. Copy it in your account on the Connect tab with the «Copy for …» button and send it to yourself by whatever opens on the television: email, a messenger, a note in the cloud. From there it can be copied and pasted into the app rather than typed. Android TV also supports keyboard apps that turn a phone into a remote with proper text entry.

autoConnect.title: Connecting automatically
autoConnect.body: Once it is set up, turn on auto-connect in the app — the tunnel then comes up by itself when the television does, with no remote involved. That matters more than it sounds: a television is usually shared, and a manual connection step becomes a source of questions. The server list refreshes itself from the subscription, so nothing has to be reconfigured when new countries appear.

why-vpn-slows-down.title: Why a VPN slows your connection, and what to do
why-vpn-slows-down.excerpt: Some speed loss on a VPN is unavoidable, but how much depends on what you chose.
why-vpn-slows-down.intro: Every VPN slows a connection down — the traffic no longer goes directly but through an intermediate server. The question is by how much: the gap between a careful setup and a careless one runs into multiples.

distance.title: Distance to the server
distance.body: The dominant factor is physical distance. Traffic to the Netherlands and back covers a few thousand extra kilometres, and that adds latency no amount of optimisation removes. From Moscow to a European server the ping usually sits at 40-60 ms against 5-15 ms direct. Page loads barely notice; games and video calls do. The rule is simple: pick the nearest country.

protocol.title: The protocol and its overhead
protocol.body: Every protocol adds its own share of bookkeeping. Older designs like OpenVPN over TCP give up as much as 20% of throughput: encryption, encapsulation, and TCP over TCP — the well-known problem where two retransmission mechanisms fight each other. Hysteria2 runs over UDP and avoids that entirely, with overhead closer to 5%. That, rather than its being newer, is why we made it the default.

packetLoss.title: Packet loss, the hidden cause
packetLoss.body: If speed drops in bursts rather than evenly, packet loss is almost certainly the cause. Over TCP each loss stalls the stream until retransmission, and at 2-3% loss speed falls by multiples rather than percentages. Ping will tell you: if some packets never come back, you have found it. Hysteria2 holds up considerably better in those conditions, because it recovers losses without stalling the other streams.

provider.title: How a network treats different protocols
provider.body: On some networks one kind of traffic moves slower than another: UDP may be rate-limited or given a lower priority than TCP, for example — or the other way round. It is hard to spot: the connection works, only slowly. The tell is that VPN speed is consistently low at any hour and on any server while direct speed is fine. Switching protocol helps: if Hysteria2 over UDP is slow, try VLESS over TCP, and the other way round.

whatToDo.title: What to check, in order
whatToDo.body: Measure your speed without the VPN first — without a baseline there is nothing to compare against. Then switch to the nearest country, which is often enough on its own. Next try the other protocol for the same country: a large difference means your network treats UDP and TCP differently. And check the time of day — evening congestion on the backbone produces a dip that has nothing to do with the VPN.

subscription-link-explained.title: What a subscription link is and how it works
subscription-link-explained.excerpt: One address instead of a config file per device. Here is what is inside it and why it is the better arrangement.
subscription-link-explained.intro: Modern VPN services hand out a single link rather than configuration files. The app downloads the server list from it and keeps that list current. Here is how that works and why it is an improvement.

whatItIs.title: What it is technically
whatItIs.body: A subscription link is an ordinary HTTPS address holding a text list of servers. The app requests it, receives a set of addresses with their connection parameters, and shows them to you as a list of countries. The format is standardised — INCY, Hiddify, v2rayNG, Streisand and a dozen other apps all understand it. That is why one link works everywhere and you are not tied to any particular client.

whyOneLink.title: Why it beats config files
whyOneLink.body: It used to be a separate configuration file per device, and adding a server meant redoing every one of them. With a link that disappears: we add a country on our side and the app picks it up on its next refresh. Setting up a new device is pasting one address rather than moving files around. And when a server has to be taken out of rotation it simply leaves the list, with nothing required from you.

howItUpdates.title: How the refresh works
howItUpdates.body: The app re-fetches the link on a schedule, usually every few hours. Along with the server list come housekeeping values: how much traffic you have used, when the subscription ends, the name of the service. That is why the app shows an accurate expiry without your opening the account page. One consequence matters: add the link as a subscription rather than as a single server. Added the second way, the app remembers one address and stops refreshing.

security.title: The link is a credential
security.body: The link carries a unique token — thirty-two random bytes by which the server recognises your account. No password travels with it, but the link itself is equivalent to access: anyone holding it can connect. So do not publish it or paste it into open chats. If it does leak, your account page has a rotate button: the old link stops working immediately and you add the new one on your own devices.

otherApps.title: It is not only for INCY
otherApps.body: We recommend INCY because we have tested it on every platform, iPhones and televisions included. But the subscription format is a common one, and the same link goes into Hiddify, v2rayNG, Streisand, NekoBox and Clash Meta. Your account page has a separate button for copying the plain link — it differs from the INCY button, which carries a scheme only that app understands. If you prefer another client, nothing stops you using it.

vpn-iphone-ipad.title: How to set up a VPN on iPhone and iPad, step by step
vpn-iphone-ipad.excerpt: Install the free INCY app, add one link from your account and connect. Plus Russian sites going direct, ad blocking and the device limit.
vpn-iphone-ipad.intro: On iPhone and iPad GnomeVPN runs through INCY, a free app from the App Store. Setup comes down to one link from your account: once it is added, the app shows every country and both protocols, and the list keeps itself current from then on. Here is what to tap, step by step, and what to watch for.

whatYouNeed.title: What you need
whatYouNeed.body: An iPhone or iPad on a current iOS, the INCY app, and an account on our site with an active subscription or free day. The free day is given once, after you confirm your email, and needs no card; the subscription terms and prices are on the <pricing>pricing page</pricing>. INCY comes from the App Store and needs no account of its own: it has no servers, it shows the ones your link delivers. Without a subscription or a free day the link is still added, but the server list stays empty.

addingLink.title: Adding the link
addingLink.body: Open your account in a browser on the same iPhone: the Connect tab, With a link, INCY. The shortest way is the Open in INCY button: the link is copied, the app opens and adds the subscription by itself. If INCY does not open, press Copy for INCY, then in the app tap + and choose import from clipboard. iOS may ask whether to allow pasting from another app — allow it. What the link is and why one link covers every device is explained in <subscription-link-explained>the post on subscription links</subscription-link-explained>.

firstConnection.title: The first connection
firstConnection.body: Once imported, INCY shows the list of countries, and each country appears twice: Hysteria2 and VLESS, with the protocol labelled on every entry. Start with Hysteria2 — it is faster, on mobile data especially. On the first connection iOS asks to allow adding a VPN configuration and to confirm it with your passcode or Face ID; without that the tunnel cannot come up. Once INCY shows you are connected, open the <status>server status page</status> and press Check connection: it tells you whether your traffic goes through GnomeVPN, and through which country.

routingAndAds.title: Russian sites and ads
routingAndAds.body: By default Russian sites go around the VPN: banks, Gosuslugi, marketplaces and everything on .ru, .su and .рф see your usual address, so there is no need to switch the VPN off for them. In your account, on the Connect tab under Routing, you can turn that off and turn ad blocking on. The list of ad domains there is short on purpose: a VPN extension on iPhone has a hard memory limit, and a huge list would get the tunnel quietly shut down by the system. AdGuard's DNS filter catches the rest. INCY applies the settings on its next subscription refresh — pull the server list down to apply them now.

otherDevices.title: iPad, Mac and other devices
otherDevices.body: On iPad everything is the same: INCY from the App Store and the same link from your account. Each device takes its own place in the subscription — two by default — and one you no longer use can be removed on the Devices tab or with /devices in the Telegram bot. Make sure HWID sending is on in INCY's subscription settings: without it a new device gets no servers. A Mac has its own <vpn-windows-macos>guide for computers</vpn-windows-macos>, and Apple TV the <vpn-android-tv>guide for televisions</vpn-android-tv>. And if something will not connect, go through <vpn-not-connecting>the checklist</vpn-not-connecting>.

vpn-android.title: How to set up a VPN on Android: phone, tablet and Android TV
vpn-android.excerpt: Install INCY from Google Play, add the subscription with one button and set the phone up so the VPN does not drop on its own. Plus a word on Android TV.
vpn-android.intro: On Android GnomeVPN connects through the free INCY app. If you open your account on the same phone, the subscription goes in with one button — nothing to copy or paste. Below: installing, the first connection, and the settings that keep the VPN from dropping on its own.

installing.title: Installing
installing.body: Install INCY from Google Play — the app is free and needs no sign-up. If the device has no Google Play, check INCY's own site, which lists the other ways to install it. Another subscription app works too — Hiddify, v2rayNG, NekoBox and Clash Meta read the same link — but the steps below are written for INCY: it is the only one where the routing switches in your account take effect. Every download link is on the <setup>setup page</setup>.

addingLink.title: The subscription in one tap
addingLink.body: Open your account in a browser on the same phone: the Connect tab, With a link, INCY. Press Open in INCY — the link is copied, the app opens and adds the subscription with every server. If INCY does not open, the link is already on the clipboard: tap + in the app and choose import from clipboard. Without an active subscription or free day the server list stays empty. The free day is switched on in your account once your email is confirmed, and the subscription terms and prices are on the <pricing>pricing page</pricing>.

firstConnection.title: The first connection
firstConnection.body: Pick a country and connect. Android asks once for permission to set up a VPN connection — confirm it, or the tunnel will not come up. Each country has two entries: Hysteria2 over UDP and VLESS over TCP. Start with Hysteria2, and if the connection will not establish — on office Wi-Fi, say — switch to VLESS for the same country. How the two differ is covered in <hysteria2-vs-vless>the post on Hysteria2 and VLESS</hysteria2-vs-vless>. Russian sites go direct by default, and ad blocking can be turned on in your account, under Routing.

stayingConnected.title: Keeping the VPN on
stayingConnected.body: Some Android skins save battery aggressively and close background apps, tunnel included. If the VPN disappears while the phone sits idle, exclude INCY from battery optimisation in its app settings. The system VPN settings also have an Always-on VPN option: with it Android brings the tunnel back up by itself after a restart. The exact path depends on the manufacturer — usually somewhere under network or connections. The server list keeps refreshing on its own schedule, so new countries appear without anything from you.

tvAndTablets.title: Android TV and tablets
tvAndTablets.body: On a tablet everything works as on a phone. On an Android TV set INCY installs from Google Play right on the screen, and there is no need to type the link with the remote: open your account on your phone, press QR code on the Connect tab and scan it in INCY on the television. Every device — phone, tablet, television — takes its own place in the subscription; remove the ones you no longer use on the Devices tab. Televisions are covered in detail in the <vpn-android-tv>Android TV and Apple TV guide</vpn-android-tv>.

vpn-windows-macos.title: How to set up a VPN on Windows and macOS, step by step
vpn-windows-macos.excerpt: Download INCY for Windows or Mac, paste the link from your account and connect. What to do when an office network will not connect, and what can replace INCY.
vpn-windows-macos.intro: On a computer GnomeVPN runs through the same INCY app as on a phone; the only difference is that the link is pasted by hand, because a computer has no button that opens the app for you. It takes a couple of minutes. Here is installing on Windows and macOS, the first connection and the fallbacks.

download.title: Where to download
download.body: The installers are on the <setup>setup page</setup>: an .exe for Windows and a .dmg for Apple Silicon Macs — every Mac with an M1 chip or newer. On those Macs INCY is in the App Store as well. For Ubuntu and Debian there is a .deb package in the same place. The app is free and needs no account of its own: the only account is on our site, where your subscription lives. Download INCY from our page or the app's official site rather than from a third-party build.

installing.title: Installing
installing.body: On Windows run the installer and approve the administrator prompt: the rights are needed to create the network adapter the tunnel runs through. On a Mac open the .dmg file and drag INCY into Applications. On the first connection the system may ask for confirmation or an administrator password once more — that is expected, the VPN connection cannot be created without it. From then on the app updates itself, so there is no reinstalling when a new version comes out.

addingLink.title: Adding the link
addingLink.body: Open your account in a browser: the Connect tab, With a link, INCY, then Copy for INCY. In INCY press + and paste the link. Add it as a subscription rather than as a single server — that way the country list updates itself and the app shows when your subscription ends. If the list is empty, check in your account that a subscription or a free day is active: without one the link delivers no servers. Terms and prices are on the <pricing>pricing page</pricing>.

officeNetworks.title: Connecting, and office networks
officeNetworks.body: Pick a country and connect. Every country has two entries: Hysteria2 over UDP and VLESS over TCP. At home start with Hysteria2; at the office or in a hotel, where UDP is often closed, go straight to VLESS — it runs over TCP on port 443, the port HTTPS sites use. Why, and what else such networks do, is in <vpn-not-working-hotel-wifi>the post on hotel and office networks</vpn-not-working-hotel-wifi>. Russian sites go direct by default in INCY on a computer too; the switch is in your account, under Routing.

alternatives.title: If INCY is not for you
alternatives.body: The same link works in Hiddify on Windows and macOS, and in Streisand on a Mac. If you want WireGuard, create a config in your account: on Windows WireSock Secure Connect opens it best and can send only chosen programs through the VPN; on a Mac use the official WireGuard app. Configs and their limits are covered in <wireguard-router-config>the WireGuard post</wireguard-router-config>. A computer takes one place in the subscription, just like a phone.

wireguard-router-config.title: WireGuard on a router or in an app: getting the config
wireguard-router-config.excerpt: How to create a WireGuard config in your account or the Telegram bot, load it into a router or an app, and how it differs from the subscription link.
wireguard-router-config.intro: The main way to connect to GnomeVPN is the subscription link in INCY. A router or a WireGuard app cannot read a link, though: it needs a .conf file. You can get one in your account or from the Telegram bot. Here is where the config comes from, where to load it and what its limits are.

whenToUse.title: When WireGuard is the right call
whenToUse.body: WireGuard is not part of the subscription, and that is deliberate. The protocol is simple and fast, but easy to recognise, and on mobile networks it often will not connect. So we hand it out as a separate config for two cases: a router that should carry the whole home network, and an app that speaks nothing but WireGuard. For a phone or a computer INCY is the easier choice: one link carries every country, Hysteria2 and VLESS, and Russian sites go direct. If a config will not connect, try INCY — how the protocols differ is in <hysteria2-vs-vless>the post on Hysteria2 and VLESS</hysteria2-vs-vless>.

gettingConfig.title: Where to get the config
gettingConfig.body: In your account open the Connect tab and choose With a config. Pick a country, name the device — Router, say — and press Create. The config can be downloaded as a .conf file or opened as a QR code to scan with a phone. The /wireguard command in the Telegram bot does the same and sends the file straight to the chat. Configs are available while a subscription or a free day is active. A server that is not answering right now cannot be picked in the form, and its state is shown on the <status>server status page</status>.

router.title: A router
router.body: Keenetic, OpenWrt and MikroTik can all act as a WireGuard client. In the router's web interface find the WireGuard connections section and upload the .conf file — or copy its fields over by hand: the keys, the address, the server and the port. Once it is on, every device on the home network goes through the VPN, the TV and the set-top box included, and the router takes a single place in your subscription limit. Keep in mind that the config sends all traffic through the tunnel, Russian sites included: the “Russian sites — direct” switch applies in INCY only.

apps.title: Apps
apps.body: On Windows WireSock Secure Connect works best: it imports the .conf and can send only chosen programs through the VPN. On iPhone and Android, AmneziaVPN: the config goes in as a file or by scanning the QR code, and the app has its own per-site split tunnelling. On macOS, Linux and anywhere the first two do not run, the official WireGuard app; on Linux it is enough to put the file in /etc/wireguard and run wg-quick up with the config name. The file name becomes the tunnel name, which is why we keep it within the 15 characters Windows and Linux allow. Links to the apps are on the <setup>setup page</setup>.

limits.title: Limits
limits.body: One config is one device and one country. To change country, create another config and delete the old one: each takes a place in your device limit. Do not load one config onto several devices — it is made for one. A deleted config stops working within a few minutes and cannot be restored, and its place is freed. Rotating the subscription link does not touch configs. When the subscription ends, configs are switched off and come back with the renewal; if the extra device places you bought run out, the configs past the limit are deleted. The rest is in the <faq>FAQ</faq>.

vpn-not-connecting.title: VPN will not connect: what to check, in order
vpn-not-connecting.excerpt: The subscription, a refresh in the app, the other protocol, the status page, the device limit and a new link — the checks that settle almost every case.
vpn-not-connecting.intro: A VPN that will not connect usually comes down to one of a few simple causes, and each takes a minute to check. Work down the list from the top: the checks run from the most common causes to the rarer ones. If none of it helps, the last section says how to write to us so we can sort it out faster.

accessAndRefresh.title: The subscription is active, and the app knows it
accessAndRefresh.body: Open your account and the Subscription tab: it shows whether a subscription or a free day is active. Without one the link delivers no servers and the app's list is empty. If you have just paid or renewed, the app may not know yet — refresh the subscription: in INCY with the refresh button or by pulling down on the server list. Read the message from GnomeVPN in the app too, if there is one: it usually names the cause — the subscription has ended, every place is taken, or the servers for a new device are still being prepared and a refresh in a minute will bring them.

protocolOrCountry.title: Another protocol or another country
protocolOrCountry.body: Every country in the subscription comes in two variants: Hysteria2 over UDP and VLESS + Reality over TCP. If Hysteria2 tries for a long time and gives up on a timeout, the network most likely does not pass UDP — common in offices, hotels and with some carriers. Switch to VLESS for the same country. If that does not help, try another country, and then another network — mobile data instead of Wi-Fi, for instance. More in the posts on <vpn-not-working-hotel-wifi>hotel and office networks</vpn-not-working-hotel-wifi> and on <hysteria2-vs-vless>Hysteria2 and VLESS</hysteria2-vs-vless>.

statusPage.title: The status page and the connection check
statusPage.body: The <status>server status page</status> shows whether each server is working right now: we check them every minute, and Having problems or Unavailable is a reason to pick another country until the server is back. The same page has a Check connection button: your browser asks an independent service for its address, and we compare it with the addresses of our servers. That shows whether your traffic really goes through GnomeVPN. A Russian IP-check site will not do for this: Russian sites open directly by default and see your usual address.

devicesAndLink.title: The device limit and a new link
devicesAndLink.body: A device takes a place the first time its app fetches the subscription, and there are two places by default. If they are all taken, a new device gets an empty list — remove one you no longer use on the Devices tab or with /devices in the Telegram bot. In INCY make sure HWID sending is on in the subscription settings: without it a new device is not accepted. And if the link has been rotated — in your account or with /rotate — the old one has stopped working on every device: copy the new one on the Connect tab and add it again. WireGuard configs are not affected.

support.title: If nothing helped
support.body: Write to us: your account has a Need help? block with email and Telegram, and the Telegram bot has a Support button — describe what happened and the answer comes back to the same chat. To help us sort it out faster, name the device and the app, the country and protocol you tried and the network — Wi-Fi or mobile data — and attach a screenshot of the error. We answer within a day. Many questions are already answered in the <faq>FAQ</faq>, and step-by-step setup for every platform is on the <setup>setup page</setup>.
